utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Registrar, can we have the accused brought in, please? (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First of all, good morning to the interpreters. I hope everybody can hear me. Good morning to the witness of the Prosecution -- no, not the witness of the Prosecution, I mean the members of the Prosecution. Good morning to the Defence counsel and good morning to General Blaskic. If everybody is ready, we will hear the testimony of another Court witness, and today, Mr. Fourmy, if I'm not mistaken, we shall start with Colonel Asim Koricic. It's a public hearing, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: Yes. You're right, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Then I will turn to the registrar and ask him to have the witness brought in. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can you hear me, Colonel? I will ask you a certain amount of information, not too much for reasons of security, but please remain standing and give us your name, surname, and place and date of birth, and if you still have a military rank, we'd like to know what kind of rank it is. If not, it's not necessary. Then you will read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Asim Koricic. I was born on the 18th of July, 1952, in Bihac. I have the rank of Colonel of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was demobilised sometime in May 1996.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Excuse me. The interpreter didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was demobilised in the rank of Colonel in 1996. By education, I am a mechanical engineer, and I head my own company now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you read the solemn declaration, and then you will be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, please be seated. Would you like us to use the title "Colonel" or do you want us to refer to you as "sir"? Because if I've understood you well, you're not mobilised anymore. You were a Colonel during the period in which we're interested, but would you like us to refer to you as "Colonel" or "sir"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Mr." would be appropriate. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Koricic, you've been summoned by the three Judges of this Trial Chamber in the trial of the Prosecutor against General Blaskic, who is the accused here today on your left. We wanted to hear your testimony. You will be able to express yourself freely for about 30 minutes or 45 minutes on very precise subjects, which I'll be giving you again, and then afterwards, the Prosecution will ask you a certain number of questions, the Defence will do the same, and the Judges. Mr. Koricic, we would like to know what was your role and your function when you were commanding the 7th Muslim Brigade at the end of 1992 and, above all, at the beginning of 1993. We would like you to describe the structure of the command of the 7th Muslim Brigade at the relevant times, its composition, its discipline, so we would like to have the basic structure and framework of the command of the 7th Muslim Brigade. We would like to know how it was deployed on location and what were its activities on the ground. We would like to have your impression on the conflict between the Croats and the Muslims, particularly when Mr. Totic was kidnapped, Mr. Totic and four officers, on the 15th of April, 1993. Finally, we would like to know whether you had any contacts or relationships, direct or indirect, with the accused, and we would like to know your impression about the accused. If you want to add other elements during your testimony, please do so, but, first of all, we would like you to express yourself freely, and if you find this difficult, then I will help you with questions that I will ask you. We are ready to listen to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Regarding the first question, which has to do with the organisation and structure of command of the 7th Brigade of the BH army, the 7th Brigade was a regular unit of the BH army envisaged by the organisational table, and according to that table, it is clearly indicated what the 7th Brigade stands for. It consists of battalions. There were three battalions. The battalions were then divided up into three companies. Then the companies are divided up into three platoons each. It had special units attached to headquarters. There was the reconnaissance sabotage company, the signals company, the logistics company, the military police company, and the engineers company. It had its own staff, the head of which was the chief of staff, and if there is no deputy commander, the chief of staff also acts as deputy commander. The staff consists of the heads of the different branches --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to ask you something. Are you reading a declaration or are you helping yourself with personal notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. The Tribunal wants you to express yourself freely, but, of course, you can use personal notes to refresh your memory. It seems very normal. Please go ahead. You didn't say what were your functions. Let's take this opportunity to ask you this question. What were your functions, from which date to which date, within the 7th Muslim Brigade? And then you can proceed with your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was one of the first commanders of that brigade, so I listed everyone, except myself, and that is, I omitted to say that I was the first commander. I was in command of the brigade until the 31st of March. As of the 31st of March, I was abroad throughout, so I was formally appointed to this duty for a short period of time. Shall I continue with the structure and method of command while I was there, if I may? The chiefs in logistics had to service the forces. There was the transportation, quartermasters, the technical and medical services. The way in which the unit and the command of the unit was organised was such that the commander had a collegiate body consisting of his assistants and the chief of staff. Then, according to the system of subordination, orders are passed on to the level of battalion, then from there to the company, to the platoon, and to lower levels, lower echelons. At times, the commander may directly inform somebody at a lower level, if that should prove necessary. So much about the basic structure. As for the deployment, the unit had its own area of responsibility, and this was designated by high-level commands, and its area of responsibility was Bucje, and I can show you that on the map. This was south-west of Travnik. That was the area of responsibility of the brigade, so the commander in charge has full responsibility for that area of responsibility, except if an order comes from a higher level of command or if somebody does not respect the rules and regulations. That would be all regarding the structure that I would have to say, unless, Your Honour, you have questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Not for the time being, so please proceed with the operations that were launched during the conflict between the Muslims and the Croats, and I would like to talk particularly about the incidents between the Armija and the HVO in which the 7th Muslim Brigade may have participated. I would like your point of view on the Dusina conflict in January 1993. I would like to hear you about the situation of the prisoners, particularly in the Kaonik prison, and the situation on the agreement of cease-fire signed between Mate Boban and President Izetbegovic on the 18th of April, 1993. You didn't give us the exact date of the term when you became commander. You mentioned the end of your term. You said you stayed commander until the 31st of March, but you didn't tell us when you started being a commander.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I began with the formation of the brigade, and the brigade was formed, I think it was in November 1992. I was actually acting commander, and my position was confirmed by the superior command in March, but I did have certain authority throughout this period up to the 31st of March. As regards the conflicts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You became commander, I'm talking about an operative commander, of the 7th Muslim Brigade from which date to which date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the point it was formed until the 31st of March, 1993. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, particularly on the points that I mentioned. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conflict occurred I think in February, the first conflict, in the area of the Lasva loop, as we call it, and the area of Dusina. At the time, I was in Travnik, and the unit of the 7th Muslim Brigade that was operating there, I think was the 2nd Battalion, it was in a preparatory stage working on regular duties and training, and it was used as an intervention unit because HV units, for reasons unknown to us but which were not unexpected, carried out an attack on the village of Merdani. I think this was a conflict of short duration. When I returned to the unit, I was informed that we had, I think, one or two dead, and already, the next day, it was halted through the intervention of the higher echelons, or a couple of days later -- actually, I don't quite remember. I can't be very specific about this because the order didn't come from us. That unit intervened, so I can't be very specific, and we didn't really carry out any analysis of this whole situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's all you have to say on the conflict which took place in Dusina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We're still talking about the conflict between the Croats and the Muslims. Could you talk about the kidnapping of Commander Totic and the four officers in 1993 and why they were kidnapped, and then we will talk about the prisoners and your role within the army staff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as the next question is concerned, the kidnapping of Mr. Zivko Totic, I said that I was absent at the time, so I heard about it, like many others, from the media, that something had happened. So I really can't say anything about that because I had already left Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You were not in Bosnia and Herzegovina anymore at that time. Very well. What about the treatment of prisoners in the prisons? The Judges have received a lot of information regarding this during this trial. That's why we have a lot of information, that we received through Prosecution witnesses or Defence witnesses, and a lot of problems were mentioned. That's why you're here. We need to have new light shed on this aspect of the conflict. We heard that the 7th Muslim Brigade took Croat prisoners. How were they treated? How were they detained? Were the international conventions applied? Could you give us a description of the situation until March 1993, and particularly about the music school. A lot was said about this music school.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was a prison in Zenica. That was the main prison within the territory under Bosniak control. That was the Kapadom as it was known, the correctional centre from former Yugoslavia, and all the prisoners were detained there, and that was something that we did not decide about. Whether people were taken into custody, I really couldn't tell you, because if people were detained, then this was according to the law. Whether the law was respected at all levels, I couldn't say. I would like to know the arguments of both sides. I don't know about that. As for the music school, it is still there. It is a school. I don't see what kind of a prison it could be when it doesn't even have a fence around it. Whether people were taken in there and interrogated, I don't know. I never heard about it. I don't know what happened because simply the conditions were not appropriate there for it to be used as a prison, so I don't know what the allegations are. As for the question whether we arrested Croats, I'm surprised at such a question because it was the Croats who arrested us. They were the first to put up checkpoints, that can be seen on the maps and that can be clearly indicated, and you should know that when I left Bosnia-Herzegovina, I had to take a document from the Croatian Defence Council -- I still have that document -- to be able to leave the territory. So I really don't know who was really in control. Furthermore, I could not move freely. There were units in Zenica, Travnik, and several other places, and I always had to have a document to be able to pass or to use certain roundabout ways through the mountains and the woods. Because if you took a map and if you find the main road in the direction from Doboj, you come across Zepce, which the Croats controlled. Then from Tuzla, there is Vares, which was again extremely well-organised and there was no free passage. From the southerly direction, there was Mostar, then Kiseljak. There too, free passage was not possible. Then the central part where we were. So we didn't control a single road. So to accuse us of arresting people -- of course, this is a possibility. One is free to say such a thing -- but our communications were intercepted by the HVO, and we couldn't move around without documents that they issued us with, so they imposed something upon us which we had never agreed upon. And as I said, I have a document on the basis of which I was able to pass through the territory under their control. But when you look at it, they virtually had control of everything. We only had some mountains and some side roads. So if you look at the whole picture, then you will see what the dividing lines were between us and possibly with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We had the feeling during the many discussions which took place during this trial that the detachment of the 7th Muslim Brigade was not always as official. Were all the units of the 7th Muslim Brigade attached to the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina? We think that there was two different parts within the 7th Muslim Brigade, and only one of them was attached to the 3rd Corps of General Hadzihasanovic who testified here yesterday. What's your impression on that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that that is not quite so. The unit was dispersed. A commander is able to deploy its forces as suits him best; of course, in accordance with higher level commands. So that is how we were deployed. Perhaps the other side feels that we were out of control, but we had units in Kakanj, in Zenica, in Travnik, so that if rapid deployment is resorted to, and this could be a military secret which I wouldn't like to go into, one could get the impression that they were out of control because it acted rapidly. But it was because it was deployed in such a way that it could do so. I said that all these units were in accordance with the organisational table. Military men know what that means. All the units had their organisational strength, their chain of command, and I don't know who could have said that they were not under the control of the army. The purpose behind this probably is to give the impression that we are Bosniak Muslims, European Muslims, that we were Islamists, Fundamentalists. We are people with our own religion, like all other people. We have certain knowledge like other peoples, maybe a little less so. We are a European people. I don't see why so much emphasis should be placed on the fact that it was called Muslim. Mr. President, perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I want things to be very clear. The Judges are not trying to do this, and you are not accused of anything. We are just trying to obtain a certain amount of information because somebody is accused here and he may face very heavy penalties, so it is absolutely normal that we are trying to discover the truth. By the way, I would like to tell you that your own Ministry of Defence told you that you had been a commander of the 7th Muslim Brigade between the 12th of March and the 6th of August, 1993. Therefore, their dates don't really correspond to the dates you gave us. So what is real? Who's right: your ministry, of which you're still a member, you're still a reservist colonel, or are you right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to clarify this. It is true what the papers say, what the ministry decided, that that is what they said. However, the command of the corps, that is, my superior, allowed me to go. There is also my order that I vest my powers in my deputy. He thus became the first in command. And it is true that then I left Bosnia-Herzegovina, and probably this date, August 1993, was pointed out because perhaps then this deputy of mine was automatically appointed commander, that is, the first in line, because I did not come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It does not correspond at all with the information that the Ministry of Defence of the federation gave us. In this document, it is said that Mr. Koricic was commander between the 12th of March and the 6th of August, and he was replaced on that date by Mr. Amir Kubura. But we will not linger on this. We have your testimony in the transcript. Can you give us any information on the reasons why the 7th Muslim Brigade was created? We received a lot of information on that aspect, and we would like what your impression is. We talked about the religious and cultural nature of this brigade. What was their training? What kind of discipline was applied within the 7th Muslim Brigade? We had a lot of information about all these aspects, but we would like to have your point of view.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A tactical brigade was supposed to be created that would operate in a wider region and that could intervene rapidly, and we probably succeeded in that. The brigade was established, like all other regular brigades, but it was supposed to take care of training as well which would guarantee certain rules because we did not have the opportunity, on the basis of the old rules, to find enough scope for training men who were supposed to realise what was happening to them. We suffered the most, from any point of view, because we had an approach that was a bit different to faith, different than that espoused by others, and we noticed that pretty quickly. We had to protect a great many people and buildings. We also had a cultural side committed against us. Whatever was built in the previous centuries was being destroyed. People wanted a unit to be created from the people who had fled. I also come from an area that was an enclave. We had to provide the best protection possible. We didn't know what to do. We could have only been transported to a third country and then gone back. However, there were many people who are aware of the fact that it's better to die in your own country than to be somebody's street-sweeper or to have somebody else feed you without doing a stitch of work. So, we decided to defend ourselves, and we wanted our training to be brought into line with regulations that were close to the hearts of us, the ordinary people, not to lie, not to steal, not to leave the battlefield, not to do to others what they are doing to us. We did not touch a single religious building. If somebody had done that, then we allowed the establishment of a commission, and then the perpetrators would be punished, but we did not allow such things. That's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Did you have any kind of autonomous or special training? Where was your headquarters? Was it in Zenica? We were told that you had a special training site with methods which were also very special and a little bit different to the methods used in the Armija or in the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not correct. We had regular training of 15 days at the most, and you can see this from the documents involved. It pertained to basic training in terms of handling the weaponry and pieces that we had available. I don't know what "special training" would mean. We would have to have special weapons in order to have a special unit. So we were taught how to shoot with an automatic rifle, a mortar. I don't know what this special thing could be. The training centre was usually in those units where there were battalions. For example, these were units at the level of battalion, and this is a question of morality. We paid great attention to ethics, as I mentioned previously. Of course, this is an army, and this had to be done behind closed doors, and I don't see why anybody would have access to military units, unless an international organisation expressed its wish to come and see us. Then we would show them on the basis of their own interests expressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: On that particular point, this is very interesting what you've just said, we heard testimonies, according to which representatives of the Red Cross never received the authorisation to visit prisoners, your prisoners; is that wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is there a letter that someone sent to me personally, and did I sign a paper saying that I would not allow this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You're not accused of anything, and that's not what I'm saying, Mr. Koricic. The Judges are just trying to learn more information. But during the training you had on ethics or you gave on ethics, did you teach your soldiers a certain number of international principles? Because the 7th Muslim Brigade was accused of having committed a certain number of looting crimes. Before this Chamber, some witnesses told us so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, I said at the very beginning that we were a regular unit of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the entire army was based on international rules. Of course we tried, as much as possible, to meet all these requirements. We certainly did not have anything special, except that amongst ourselves, we were perhaps different from others because we were perhaps more faithful than others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Who are the Mujahedin? Were they members of the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the problem. We are being told that we had foreigners, so to speak, in our ranks. Sometimes we'd have a logistics man who would volunteer, for example, to go to positions together with lower level units. I don't know. While I was active, I wish to inform you now that there were no conflicts with the Croatian Defence Council, except for that in Dusina, never, and if the Mujahedin were present while there were Territorial Defence staffs, if that's what they called these people, but these are mainly people who remained -- I mean, in the former Yugoslavia, people went to schools, and then there were humanitarian organisations. If I could not pass without a permit, I think that the HVO knows exactly how many people got in. I really don't know that any such person was registered in the 7th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What happened in Dusina in January happened during the period when you were commander of the 7th Muslim Brigade; am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We've heard testimonies from representatives of the ECMM, it was not the testimony of the accused, and these people then mentioned a certain number of crimes which were committed in the municipality of Dusina. You were a commander, you're not accused of anything, but we're just trying to know what happened. Could you control your soldiers? Were you in control of the situation? I would like to take this opportunity to add that, according to a certain number of testimonies, your brigade or some Mujahedins were not controlled anywhere by the commander of the Armija. You were a commander, until the 31st of March at least, but maybe until the month of August, could you talk more precisely about the events which took place in Dusina, more precisely than at the beginning? What happened in Dusina? Do you know? You were a commander at the time. I'd like to repeat that you're not here as an accused, you're here as a witness, but you've taken the oath. Let me remind you of this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that something had happened out there. I mean, had I heard that something had happened there, I would have initiated proceedings had I received information about this in detail from the appropriate institutions, but I did not receive any request. Intensity was short. You know, it's not that simple for me to try to remember now everything that happened. Well, yes, you can forget, but I know for sure that something had happened because people were talking, and they were saying all sorts of things, but who did what, that I do not know. Not a single verified official organisation came and told me that something had happened truly and that I was supposed to take action. So the only thing I know is that something was being talked about those days. There were some objections, but no objections were raised officially to me as commander so that I would establish a commission and -- I mean, of course, I would have done that. So I really cannot give you an explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So you never learned anything about what happened in Dusina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, believe me, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: If I understood you well, the relationship you had with Mr. Hadzihasanovic was a normal hierarchial relationship between a superior and a subordinate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One hundred per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You received your orders from General Hadzihasanovic, combat technical orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: My last question: Your strategic option, was it yours? Was it General Hadzihasanovic's? Did you have your own objectives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I had said that we had subordination in the army system, then it is impossible without the approval of the superior command. For the use of every unit, one has to write a request in order to use that unit, and then one has to explain how one intends to do that. In order to get into somebody else's zone, again, you have to ask the superior command to grant that request of yours, so very often, our units were attached to others. Personally, I had no ideas, except for the basic idea we all had, and that was to defend ourselves from all this suffering, to organise some kind of living conditions as much as possible, and that's it. That would be all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I understand. Do you have any information about brutal attacks which would have been launched in the municipality of Busovaca by the ABiH with the support of the Mujahedins against the Croat population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really did not hear of the Mujahedin attacking Busovaca. Perhaps they called us the Mujahedin because, as we said a few minutes ago, the 2nd Battalion was operating in these regions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This will be my last question. The Mujahedin were attached, or those individuals who were called the Mujahedin, were attached to the 7th Muslim Brigade or were they an autonomous group? I didn't really understand what was their status.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were there because they wanted to give humanitarian help, and perhaps they came. These were certain groups of foreigners, and perhaps they would come to us too. Perhaps that was the link. Maybe they had an escort. I don't know what the HVO did. Probably their security would, perhaps, follow these people, I imagine they did, because they controlled them from the moment they crossed the border, and then these people probably brought us appropriate assistance and also assistance to units, and then it is accentuated. They went to see these foreigners and they went to see these others. These were just their assumptions. We were a regular Bosnian unit, and we carried out our regular duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. When they were placed under your orders, Mr. Koricic, you gave them orders, or did they operate autonomously without any command structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were never under our command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Therefore, they were on your territory, they are not under the orders of the HVO, they are not under your orders or the orders of General Hadzihasanovic, who paid them? A lot was said about them, and not only by Defence witnesses but also by international observers. It seems that they received financial support from Islamic countries, powers from the Islamic world. You don't know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That they received support from Islamic countries, I don't believe that. Perhaps they had the support and help of some people, some persons, but that there were some groups in our territory, please, there were about 200.000 of us. We're not talking about the army now. We are talking about some 20-odd foreigners. Of course, if they did something, they should be held accountable, but, please, we did not call these people, we did not tell them, "Please come here and let's get organised." I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: There were only around 20? There were only 20 Mujahedins, 20 Mujahedins while you were a commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not with me. I would pass, you see, and I would see something in certain areas where they were, but I did not see that these were groups, and there weren't that many. There were perhaps 20, 30. I don't know the number. I couldn't establish that, and I don't know about that. You know, these areas -- I mean, I think that they were involved in humanitarian matters. They would get married --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Koricic, you're saying that your brigade was a regular unit, that the soldiers were trained a little bit differently than other units, particularly units pertaining to the army corps of General Hadzihasanovic. You mentioned the rather cultural/religious nature of the brigade and you mentioned ethics. However, you accept people who say they apply the same ethics, since they are Muslims and they are financially supported by other countries; they arrive on the territory; you're not trying to control them, you're not trying to integrate them within your own structure; you leave them to operate like this. Above all, when you learned that they may have committed a certain number of atrocities, you just leave them alone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not take anyone in. Such people did not stay in our units. These people could not get organised. This was a regular unit. From the point of view of formation, this is not possible. We never gave a single dinar to pay such persons. We were not armed with special weapons. We had basic weapons like everybody else, those who had the possibility of arming themselves then. As for the control of civilian territory, it is well-known, according to the law, who was in charge of that. We cannot do the work of the MUP. After all, how did the HVO let these foreigners cross their territory? Probably as humanitarian persons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You're not answering my question. It seems that the presence of Mujahedins was confirmed, it was verified, and not only ten people were mentioned to us. So if you, commander of the 7th Brigade, who, by the way, you're not even able to say that you were commander from the exact date to another exact date. Of course, I understand that we may have even more doubts on the presence of Mujahedins on your territory. By the way, I thought that your testimony would be free, but I had to ask you a certain number of questions. I will not turn to my colleagues now because they will ask questions at the end, but I shall now turn to the Prosecution for some 30 minutes. Would that be enough, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, good morning. Counsel, good morning. Mr. Koricic, good morning. We have no questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I shall now turn to Mr. Nobilo. This is not a cross-examination, Mr. Koricic. You are a Court witness. It will be, therefore, only questions asked by the Prosecution or the Defence and then the questions of the Judges will follow. Mr. Nobilo, how much time do you need? Half an hour? Will that be enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I hope so. About 30 minutes. That will be sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We shall now hear your questions until the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Colonel Koricic, I am Anto Nobilo. This is my colleague, Russell Hayman. We are the Defence counsel. And I should like to ask you a few questions now. Why was the 7th Muslim Brigade called a Muslim Brigade while all the others were called light brigades or mountain brigades? Where does that specific difference come from?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I should like to clarify matters. The question related to the 7th Muslim Brigade and to say a few words: In the former state, we had the republics. We had Slovenia, and that was a Slovene, Croatia was a Croat, Serbia was a Serb. When you came to Bosnia, you had the nation called the Muslim, and that is a very broad notion, "the Muslim," just as the Croatian-Muslim conflict, the term given there, that is very wrong, because it is a Croatian-Bosniak conflict. Because we could then say, if we followed that logic, and say a Bosnian-Catholic conflict, and that would not correspond to the situation. So then -- and the gentlemen know that there was a small "m" for "Muslim" and a big "M" for "Muslim," that is to say, denoting the religious and the national, the ethnic notion, and these are broader elaborations of the term, and that was used so that in a period of time, we could feel or come to feel that that area belonged to some, let us say, Muslims, who had not been there from time immemorial. And so we said that the brigade will be called the Muslim Brigade because there would be a little greater emphasis on religion there, and that when conditions were ripe, when it changed nationally, it wouldn't be called the Muslim but would be either called the Bosnian or Bosniak or, as it is called now, just the 7th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could somebody join the 7th Muslim Brigade who was a Catholic, for example, or an Orthodox, or not religious at all?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Well, nobody could join who was an atheist, but the other thing was unrealistic to expect under the prevailing conditions because those relationships were unrealistic, as I said, and could not have been expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber, please, whether your conception of religion and the role of religion in war and within the 7th Muslim Brigade was different from how other Bosniaks in Bosnia-Herzegovina can see this thing? Was there a qualitative difference between the two?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, probably there was. For example, we don't drink alcohol. Second, we didn't do any looting on the roads and we didn't do all the ugly things that people talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What about the other Bosniaks? Did they?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: No, but you asked me whether there were any substantial differences, and I said that the qualities we afforded were better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I'm going to repeat the question. Please listen to me carefully. Was the understanding of the role of religion within the 7th Muslim Brigade, the role of religion in wartime, was it different from the conception of religion and its role in wartime in the other brigades of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Was there a qualitative difference in understanding, and if so, in what direction?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: There are no two rules. There is just one rule when you come to religion. It is only how people accept that rule, and perhaps we accepted it -- we accepted a different approach in relation to others. I'm speaking about percentages. So I don't want to go on with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Of course, religion is one thing, but could you tell us whether you adhered to religion in stricter terms than the other religious people in the other brigades of the BH army? Were you stricter and embraced religion in a more comprehensive manner?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: You know that in the daily distribution in units, and if you don't know, then you should get to know this point, that is to say, in the -- we have prayers five times a day in our daily routine, and that was the difference. So we had more prayer than the others. That is one of the differences. Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I don't know the extent to which other units, other members of units said their prayers, whether that was regulated by the rules of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Colonel, do you know the religious laws and rules about conducting warfare?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: No, I know very little on that subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What about your teachers, the religious teachers in the 7th Muslim Brigade? Did they speak about the religious rules of conducting warfare?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Of course, religion always wishes to give encouragement to its believers at given points in time. You said a legal -- you said a religious leader. I would say a religious dignitary so --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I said religious teacher.

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Then I apologise, and that is correct, right, religious teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I'm asking you a direct question now: Were the rules of Islamic Fundamentalism, which, according to history, are not inherent in the Bosniak people, were endeavoured to be applied in the 7th Muslim Brigade with the help of foreign instructors from Arab countries?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: First and foremost, let me say that the question is a very broad one. You said Islamic Fundamentalism. I would like to hear from you what you mean by Islamic Fundamentalism.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Well, that would lead us into a lengthy debate. But let me put it this way: In your brigade, and I'm going to ask a specific question, did heavenly laws have the advantage or the laws of this earth? Would you give me a direct answer? So not roundabout, as is usual in Bosnia, but a direct answer. Which rules had the advantage?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Well, I am speaking to you as one man to another. If a man is endangered, then he might prefer death to life.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You haven't answered my question.

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: I think I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We are in a court here and have to give direct answers. I know that when you have a cup of coffee in Bosnia, you tend to philosophise a little bit. But I'm going to ask you whether, in your brigade, you adhere to heavenly laws rather than the laws of this earth?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: I said, sir, that we were a regular unit that had assignments on this earth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, please, did you teach your fighters to apply the Geneva Conventions in wartime or did you give special instructions to the Muslim fighters?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: I'm going to tell you of a personal experience of mine. I could just say "Yes," we are duty-bound to do that but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I asked you whether you gave special instructions to Muslim fighters how to behave towards civilians, prisoners, and so on. Tell us whether you had instructions of that kind.

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Let me answer in the way I would like to give you the answer. Gentlemen, if you go into battle, anybody who kills a woman, anybody who kills a child, anybody who destroys a religious building or does evil does not belong to us and I will not stand behind a man of that kind, and that is what I can say to this illustrious tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you issue in writing, that is to say, did the religious instructors give written instructions to Muslim fighters which referred only to the Muslim fighters?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Would you clarify what you mean when you say "Muslim"?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to read a part of a Defence document, 184, D184. I apologise, there is a title in Arabic, first of all, and then it says "Basic Instructions to a Muslim Fighter," and it speaks about the Sheheeds, permits for parents and so on. I'd like to ask the usher to come and get this document. It is D184. Take a look at the whole document, and I am just going to read a portion of it, Relationship Towards Hostile Civilians, Enemy Civilians, point 2. Take a look at point 2. (as read) "Women and children, like all the other civilians helping the enemy, can be killed and they are treated in the same way as the attackers. If needed, an abandoned house can be used for defence." This was distributed in Travnik, which is where you were the commander.

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: I do not see a stamp of the 7th Muslim Brigade, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What is the stamp here? Can you identify it? Can you read out what it says on the stamp?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: I just see that it says MOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Have you ever seen a stamp of this kind before?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: This stamp was never seen in our units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you ever see this kind of instruction to Muslim fighters and was it distributed to your soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: I am not an expert in religious rules and instructions. This was probably copied from religious literature and religious instructions somewhere, and you can probably buy instructions of that kind throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you adhere to the rules and regulations as prescribed by religion in warfare?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Well, I told you that we adhered to rules that were binding upon us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That answer can be taken twofold.

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: So you want me to answer and to tell you something that I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I asked a very clear question: Did you adhere to religious rules connected to warfare?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Religious rules were not binding for us in the sense of a law, that we should be held responsible, so I don't see why I should now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. Let us proceed. You had an Emir of a unit, and the word "Emir," the term "Emir," I think means, in a language we both understand, means "Ruler," Mahmut Efendija Karalic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Where did you happen to read that, that he was a member of our formation?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: He established you, he financed you, and I'm just asking you whether you know him and whether he had any role in the establishment of your unit. Was he the Emir of the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: I know him. He could have been, he might have been somebody who we had contacts with --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What kind of answer is that, "He could have been," "He might have been"? You were the commander of the 7th Muslim Brigade. You have to tell us what links you had with him, what your connection with him was and what relationship you had with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Wait a second, please. I first would like Mr. Nobilo to ask his questions -- and please, Mr. Nobilo, give the witness the time to answer -- and I would also turn to the witness and ask him to focus on the questions asked by the Defence and to give them a proper answer. I would like to remind the witness that he is still under oath. Please, Mr. Nobilo, rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let me ask this once again: What was the role of Emir Mahmut Efendija Karalic in the creation and organisation and work of the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: His role was logistical because an Islamic centre had been set up for assistance to the peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was set up in Zenica, where the No. 1 man was Mahmut Karalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Where did the Islamic Centre for assistance to Zenica get its resources from, funded from, led by Karalic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: You should ask the Islamic centre that and Mr. Karalic. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What about the humanitarian officers that passed you by? Were they on their way to that Islamic centre?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Probably they were, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that your battalion went to Dusina and that they committed crimes there but that you were not in command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: I did not issue an order of that kind because I was at that time, I think, in the Travnik region when the attack came.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: If you did not issue an order to your battalion, who could have issued orders? Who was your superior?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: There was no need for anybody to issue an order above me. The order could have been issued by the chief of staff in my absence. He could have issued an order of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When information reached you that a crime had been committed in Dusina but nobody informed you of that officially, did you not consider it your duty as commander of the brigade to conduct an investigation? It was your unit. They were not some far off units. They were people under your direct command. Did you ever conduct an investigation into that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: You must know, sir, that I did not get this information immediately. A considerable amount of time went by, and it was from contacts, and we heard from your people that something had, in fact, happened, but this was quite a lot later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: First of all, there are no "my people" in Dusina. I have no relatives in Dusina, so they are not my people. That's one point. Another point is that you left in March 1993, so that was a period of two months, but when the information reached you, did you conduct an investigation and did you feel duty-bound to conduct an investigation?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I might have heard that when I came back to the country, when I heard about these contacts, and what was his name, Zeko, there was a man called Zeko from the HVO, and he said, "You know, Asim, perhaps there are some problems," and I said, "Really? Well, if there are, then let's have a request for something," but as I wasn't the officer on duty and I had no duty --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us forget Dusina for a minute. Between Kacuni and Bilalovac, that is to say, between the municipalities of Vitez and Kiseljak, Gusti Grab, for example, Oseliste, and the other Croatian villages were set fire to, people were expelled, and that was done by your unit?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: In that period?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, in that same period, the time of Dusina, in fact, in those days.

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: I do not know anything about reports of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: They are reports of a joint commission. Representing the BH army, we had Mr. Dzemo Merdan, and representing the Croatian side, we had Mr. Franjo Nakic under the auspices of the international organisations, and they ascertained what had happened, that several hundred Croatian houses had been set ablaze.

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. Did you say Dzemo Merdan? Dzemo Merdan did not make any comments, did not tell me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: He did not inform you about that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: You see, we were left without many houses ourselves, and it is difficult, unless a commission ascertains this and we go down the lines, subordination, and if you say you had this gentleman who asked this, therefore, and made this demand, then Mr. Merdan should have come to my office, sat at my table, and told me what he had to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The joint commission went house by house and listed all the burnt houses, and I want to know whether Dzemo Merdan informed you of that.

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: I received no official information, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How do you explain that your ministry disposed of data and information, that until August, you were the commander, and you say that you had left the country. If you had actually left the country, who allowed you to do so, and who allows the function of brigade commander to be filled so that you could go abroad? Who is the competent authority to do that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: First of all, the ministry is the higher command. Sarajevo was in an encirclement, under siege, but it is the corps commander who issued permission for me to go abroad either temporarily or permanently. According to our rules and regulations, I would have to propose somebody to take my place and be my deputy, and the next man in line was the chief of staff, if there is no deputy commander of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you do all of this in writing?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: This was prepared in writing. A request is put to the army, and I had to make a request of this kind to go to the HVO department who would then issue the necessary documents to me for passage through territory controlled by it, and that was all done on the basis of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How can you then explain that the ministry, and you sent them all these documents, held -- that kept you commander until August, and then five months before that, you were not in command, as you say?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Because, according to the regulations of the BH army, six months is a maximum time period, and it is not the ministry that is responsible for a time period of six months, that is to say, the higher command. After six months, then automatically, the ministry can make its move and take the necessary steps, and a new request is submitted within that time period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But if you made all these requests to the ministry, as you say, then the ministry must have recorded that and recorded that you had left and were not de facto a commander. Do you not consider that to be an important point?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: No, and I can also allow lower commanders to do the same. It is the system of subordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But you've just said that you left after you had informed everybody and received legal permission?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Yes, but you were not listening. The ministry is not duty-bound to solve cases of this kind at the level -- this is resolved at the corps level or brigade level and lower down the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you left, who took over? Who became the responsible officer?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: The rules said that it was the chief of staff, and that is Mr. Amir Kubura. Mr. Amir Kubura was appointed commander, and also the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We'll ask him that. Now I want to ask you about the music school building. Was not your command in the music school in Zenica, the command or the headquarters of the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: No, it was never in the music school, but it was at the secondary educational centre, that is to say, at the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What formation was in Zenica in the music school building?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: I think it was the department which belonged to the 2nd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Of which Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: The 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So your unit was in the music school, it was located in the music school?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Before that, we had units of the Muslim forces. Now, how these were transformed, this took place in a shorter period of time, and who inherited these units and how they were deployed and how the commands went, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But you have just said that a portion of the 2nd Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade was located in the music school building.

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Has the music school got any basement or cellars and have you ever toured them?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is it correct that Alija Izetbegovic gave you a flag when you established the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: That is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did he tour the 7th Muslim Brigade in the sports hall in Zenica in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: I think this was in 1993, in the winter of 1993, autumn, winter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The end of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Thereabouts, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You weren't at that review, were you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: No, I was not. I was doing something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you attend the review?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How do you say that you were present and weren't present and didn't belong there in the autumn of the -- that you didn't belong to the 7th Muslim Brigade in the autumn? Were you in uniform?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was in uniform, and the 7th Corps was being established, and that is where I was, and I was invited as its first commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you have any function to perform? Did you report on the occasion?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: No, never. With my departure, I was never on duty at the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But the review we're talking about, was there any ceremonial function that you performed?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is it true that the 7th Muslim Brigade was, in fact, directly subordinate to Alija Izetbegovic as president of the Bosnian presidency?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: We did not have any guards brigades, as did some other countries, that is to say, that Alija Izetbegovic did not directly command the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The El Mujahed detachment, what was the relationship between the 7th Muslim Brigade and the El Mujahed detachment?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: It was as I have already said, a humanitarian connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But I'm asking you about the El Mujahed detachment. It is difficult that a detachment can engage only in humanitarian work.

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: We had relations with the El Mujahed, as we had with the other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who was the El Mujahed detachment subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Not to us. Otherwise, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did it function within the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether it was in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Probably, that is where it was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But, Colonel, asked by the Judges, you said that there were 20 or 30 humanitarian individuals, and now you say there was a whole detachment, a whole El Mujahed detachment. A detachment is a very large number of people. It is not the 20 humanitarian workers that you mentioned a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: If you're thinking about foreigners, I heard about it, I don't know, but I heard that other Bosnians joined those units, and probably it had grown to that number. You know, there were 1.000 individuals, 300 foreigners and 700 Bosniaks. If that were the case, then it would have been called a brigade, but I'm sure the number wasn't that large. That is what I assume. But as far as foreigners are concerned, I really don't know how many there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Colonel, I'm now going to read the results of a military unit that you trained. You trained them in humanitarian conduct. In a military operation in June 1993 when allegedly you were not in command, in the Travnik municipality alone, 427 soldiers were killed, 157 civilians were killed, 30 civilians were killed by sniper --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel, are you reading from an exhibit? If so, can we have the exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No. No, these are not exhibits. They are just my notes which emanate from all the Defence exhibits. If we were to unify all the Defence exhibits, those were the facts and figures that you would arrive at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon, for this precision. Now we know that that is not an exhibit, and Mr. Harmon was right in asking this question. We will take a break. Please finish on that point, Mr. Nobilo, and then we will take a break, if you need some more minutes to end.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In June, July, and August, when you allegedly were no longer the commander of the 7th Muslim in Travnik, the results of those operations were 427 killed soldiers, 157 killed civilians, 1.000 wounded persons, 1.500 burned down Croatian homes, 3.100 devastated buildings, et cetera, et cetera, and some villages, like Grahovcici, Donja Maljina, Guca Gora, Bikosi, Sadici, Gornja Puticevo, Rudnik, Bila, Cupa, and so on, were burnt down. About 50 villages between Zenica and Travnik, Croatian villages, were totally burned down. Tens of thousands of people abandoned Travnik municipality, Croats, in front of the 7th Muslim. You were not in command then, but my question is: Is that what you taught your combatants?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: My dear sir, you must know that the army is never trained to serve coffee only. Let me explain myself. It is important for the army to be trained in accordance with international rules, and I think that these operations were within the bounds of those international rules and standards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. I'm sorry, Mr. Koricic, you didn't give a proper answer to the question that was asked. Please, when you turn to Mr. Nobilo, call him "Mr. Nobilo" and not "my dear sir," which is not proper in this Tribunal. I would say exactly the same thing if you used this term for the Judges or members of the Office of the Prosecutor. We will take a break right now, and then we will resume. Mr. Nobilo, do you need some more time to finish?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I'll be very brief, just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: A 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please, let's have the accused brought in. The hearing is resumed. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, we shall hear the remaining questions you have. You can ask these questions until 12.00. Will that be sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I shall be very brief. About ten minutes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Colonel, could you tell us when you returned to the country? You said that you left at the end of March 1993. When did you go back?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: I think it was sometime in October or November.

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you have any record of that in your passport, any evidence?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Will you tell us what positions you held when you returned?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: None. I was appointed to a group that would form the 7th Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When did that begin?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Immediately after that. After the review that you mentioned, sometime then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you tell us the deployment of your brigade in '93, before you left? You told us about the area of responsibility, but the actual deployment, where was it actually deployed?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: We said before -- you want me to tell you the commands?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Because it was dispersed, one command of one battalion was in Zenica, another command in Travnik, another one in Kakanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was that in the elementary school in Kakanj?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: I think it was across the road. I don't know the name of the school, the upper part of that school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Dobrina is its name, something like that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you mention Zepce?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: No, no. We were not deployed in Zepce.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What about Fojnica?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: No. I just told you the places.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What about Biljesevo?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: No, no. The heliodrom was there, if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What about Novi Travnik, Ravno Rostovo?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a part there, but not in that period. I don't know the exact period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But Rostovo to the right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: There are two Rostovos. One is near Vakuf and one is between Novi Travnik and Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am talking about the latter, between Novi Travnik and Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you hear, when you returned, that four officers of the HVO Novi Travnik Brigade were kidnapped in Ravno Rostovo?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the Abdul Latif detachment of Mujahedin origin?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: I heard these various names, but believe me, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That detachment was accommodated in Kakanj. You never saw them?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: No, I never taught them nor did I know such a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that the 2nd Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade intervened in Dusina in January '93. Who was in command of that 2nd Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade in January '93?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: The commander of the battalion was Mr. Serif Patkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you left the position of commander of the 7th Muslim, which country did you go to?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: I lived exclusively in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: In Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were you registered there?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So you were there illegally?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Of course. What else could I be in this war?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That brings to an end my questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But let me add, I had documents as -- I beg your pardon. I am not familiar with the subordination in court. Your Honour, Mr. President, I wanted to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Don't speak of subordination here. We are not in the army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We military men are prone to use military terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I understand. Could you add the position you wanted to add?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had permission to try and organise humanitarian aid, and that is the document I used throughout in Croatia, and nobody bothered me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Koricic. I will turn towards my brother Judge Shahabuddeen. Do you have any questions, Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Colonel, would you help me to be clearer on one or two points concerning Dusina. I think you said these words: "I know for sure that something had happened." So in your mind, there was a conviction that something had happened. Did you believe that certain crimes had been committed at Dusina by your 2nd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Can I begin my answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I later learnt that something had happened in contact with this officer of the HVO, but believe me, to this day, I don't know what happened and I don't know of what magnitude it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you have been in a position to know what happened and of what magnitude it happened if you had taken steps to investigate what allegedly happened?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: No, I was not in a position to know that or to investigate it because there should have been a different set of circumstances in place for me to be able to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You had no power to inquire as to what happened even though you said that you knew for sure that something had happened?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: I learnt that very late when probably I no longer was in office and could not undertake anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, the 7th Muslim Brigade is now called the 7th Brigade. At the time in question, was there an emphasis in the 7th Muslim Brigade on ethical standards?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: No, no, we didn't have such standards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did you have ethical standards in the normal military regime relating to the brigade?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir. We were obliged to have such standards by the rules of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina which were coordinated with international rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And you did not consider that those ethical standards required you to inquire into what happened at Dusina?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Yes, but while I was in office, no information reached me about it, and that is why I didn't do anything. If such reports had reached me, I would have surely submitted a request for an investigating commission, especially if such request were to be made by a superior command, then it is doubly obligatory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: How long after the occurrence of the events at Dusina did you learn of those events?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: When I returned from the Republic of Croatia, I wanted to hear what had happened and, among other things, I had various contacts with people and they were able to tell me many things, some assumptions, some correct, I don't know, but it was roughly then that I learnt about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, how do you compute that period, the period between then, when you learnt of what had happened, and the time when those things, in fact, happened?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: It's roughly more than half a year in between.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Rodrigues, do you have any questions? Thank you, Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Koricic, I would like to go back to the creation of the 7th Muslim Brigade. In what conditions was this brigade created, and, particularly, who asked you to create the 7th Brigade? At that time, what were your functions and what was your training at the time?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: At the time, I belonged to the municipal staff of Travnik, as a man who had fled from another region. Actually, I couldn't go back to my own area because it was an enclave. At that time, brigades began to be formed, which, in my view, was a good thing undertaken by the army to improve its organisation and to deal with all these things in a better manner. At the time, it was possible to propose people to various positions. I was in the area of Karaula, which later fell into the hands of the Serb forces, and in that period, we lost control of those areas, and a large number of the army was concentrated in the area of Central Bosnia because we had lost the area from Jajce to Travnik, which is about 30 kilometres long and some 20 kilometres wide, but this was an area which gave us access to a larger town called Jajce. All the forces were concentrated there, several thousand combatants were there, and, of course, the army at that very moment formed brigades. As I was at the level of company commander in the area, and there were many troops, the decision was taken to form brigades. As I was a foreigner and these units consisted of many people from other areas, I felt closer to those units than to some local units, so I was proposed by the municipal staff, that is, Travnik, to that newly formed brigade. Other people had other proposals, and the proposal was conveyed to a higher level command, and it wasn't confirmed until March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: What about your own formation or training, rather? You went through a certain training. You had a military career, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I attended from 1967 until 1971 the Air Force Technical Military School in Rajlovac, that is, the air force, belonging to the air force, but this was not very appropriate because my work had to do with the infantry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Who gave the 7th Muslim Brigade its name?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: At the time, there were various proposals. There were suggestions that it be named after certain soldiers, after certain prominent personages, to be given names, in other words, and then the army made the right move and suggested it be given a number, which is logical, and we asked that our number be 7 because we believed that the brigade would belong in the future to a 7th refugee cause, 7, 17, 27, but we didn't succeed. It remained part of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: But who added the term "Muslim" to its name?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: At the time, this was '72, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, we hadn't resolved many things, so we didn't know how things would develop because we had many other units. There were units of heterogeneous composition with representatives of other ethnic groups, so we didn't know exactly, and we wanted to keep it national, ethnic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Therefore, the 7th Muslim Brigade was part of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You said that a Catholic could not be a member of the 7th; right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that he couldn't, but I said that it wasn't realistic, and the atmosphere was not such because there were conflicts between these ethnic groups. We were more dedicated to religion, and it was not realistic to expect someone with different views to join, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: However, in theory, a Catholic could have been a member, for instance, of the 8th or the 14th?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: He could be a member of the 7th too, if he wanted to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: It was not realistic to envisage this.

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we had very good cooperation with the HOS, the Croatian Armed Forces, which later disappeared, we don't know why, and they were of mixed composition. When Karaula fell to the Serbs, together with Mr., I think his name was Ante Prkacin --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You mentioned the HOS. What was the relationship between the 7th Brigade and MOS?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: When the 7th Muslim was formed, the MOS no longer existed because the army had been transformed and many units were disbanded, so that the MOS does not exist at the same time as the 7th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: However, maybe they were individuals, men, soldiers, weapons. Where did all these people and weapons go?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Most of them were reappointed to the 7th Muslim Brigade. Some went to their own areas, there are written traces of what happened, but a considerable number were in the 7th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Can we, therefore, claim that the HOS -- sorry, I mean the MOS, the MOS is fundamentally integrated within the structure of the 7th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: Units of the municipal staffs constituted the basis for the formation of other high-level units. Where MOS members were assigned to can be seen clearly. They too were assigned to the 7th or to some other unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Koricic, another question: Who financed the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ASIM KORICIC
utterances.text: The 7th Brigade had regular logistic support from the corps, the corps logistics, and the 7th Brigade was covered by that logistics support. As for other support, it was provided by the Islamic Centre in Zenica, which we addressed, for aid regarding the families of the killed soldiers and various other everyday problems, and we sought support wherever else we could get it, to deal with these problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: The Islamic Centre supported other brigades financially, or was it only the 7th Brigade?
