utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. I think that we will end this testimony. I remind you that you were summoned by the Judges, the Chamber, not by the Defence or the Prosecution. All you risk is perjury, and I'm reminding you of that because incrimination is within the field of responsibility of the Prosecution, not the Judges. I have only one question for you: Do you have a feeling, following the questions by Judge Rodrigues, you are aware of Merdani, and when we talk about Dusina, you talk about Merdani. Can you explain, how is it that you are familiar with what happened in Merdani, and you referred to Dusina in relation to Merdani, but you don't know what happened in Dusina? Could you explain this apparent contradiction for us?

utterances.speaker: AMIR KUBURA
utterances.text: Yes, I can explain. At that time, I was in Zenica. A person came into my office. This person told me that his two daughters were taken prisoner in the village of Merdani and that the village of Merdani was attacked by HVO units. At that time, two pictures were brought to me. I still have them. One is a picture of the village of Merdani and the other picture is a man who's fleeing the village of Merdani, and he has a cow and a dog. The conflicts started in the village, and, therefore, I got orders from the headquarters of the corps that I should attach one of my companies there. After that, I got a report that an attack was carried out in the direction of Dusina where that company of mine was and that, on that occasion, I had two of my men killed and six wounded. Apart from my unit, there was also the municipal staff unit that was there and that they also had some of their members wounded and killed, that is to say, that there were several casualties, men who were killed and wounded, in that zone. That is what I know in connection with Merdani and in connection with Dusina. Because this unit was attached to the Territorial Defence, I think they have more information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is it possible to make a link between a mission of one of your companies in Dusina and the atrocities that may have been committed there or were committed there? Is it possible to establish that link? Because, after all, the conflict had started between the HVO and the 3rd Corps of the army. Is it possible to make that link? You said that this company went towards Dusina. Is it possible to make this link, even though you, as assistant chief of staff, were not informed? I'm just asking you, "Yes" or "No," is it possible to make that link?

utterances.speaker: AMIR KUBURA
utterances.text: At that time, the company was in that zone attached to the municipal staff, and combat action was already under way, that is to say, after Merdani, combat action was already under way, and that was the zone concerned, and that is where this second attack of the HVO units was taking place. The first was against Merdani; the other one was against Dusina, that is to say, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do not talk about the HVO. We are very familiar with their operations. I am asking you whether it is possible for a company, which is, after all, under your orders, indirectly, but still under your orders, could have been in Dusina and perpetrated these atrocities, "Yes" or "No"? Is it possible, intellectually, I'm asking you? Is it possible? I'm reminding you that we are in public hearing. You were assistant chief of staff of the 7th Muslim Brigade, who shortly became commander. You knew that a company went to the region of Dusina, and there was a conflict with the Croats already, is it possible that they participated in those operations? I won't talk about crimes. Is it possible or not?

utterances.speaker: AMIR KUBURA
utterances.text: When this company came into this area, they did not start combat immediately. They were not fighting immediately. They held the line. After that, a few days later, fighting started in that direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: How did you know that it was not engaged in the fighting? How did you know that, because you were the assistant chief of staff, "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: AMIR KUBURA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So that proves that if one is assistant chief of staff of a brigade called the 7th Muslim Brigade, one does, after all, come to learn about a certain number of events, "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: AMIR KUBURA
utterances.text: Yes, and there is one more thing I wish to emphasise, if you allow me to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: AMIR KUBURA
utterances.text: The company commander, Fahrudin Camdzic, on that day went, on behalf of his zone, to negotiate with the commander of the HVO, and the HVO man said that he would negotiate then, but he was killed at that time, he was killed on that occasion, and that is when their attack started in this direction of Dusina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You see, you do know things after all, Colonel. You know much more than you have told us so far. I think we shall end your testimony. We will thank you, nevertheless, for coming all the way to The Hague, and we are going to allow you to go back to your work. We will have a 30-minute [as interpreted] break and then hear our last witness for the day. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Have the accused brought in, please. I understand that the English interpreters gave themselves ten minutes' extra break, but that's nothing serious. Let us bring in our last witness, Colonel Serif Patkovic. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Will you please tell us your full name, your rank in the army, your date and place of birth, and your current occupation, after which you will take the solemn declaration standing, and then you can be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Serif Patkovic. I am a colonel; I was in the army. I am no longer in active service. Currently I am a private businessman rearing cattle. I was born on the 5th of October, 1967, in the municipality of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Take the oath now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. I will call you Mister. You may be seated. You were a colonel at the time of the events. You are appearing before the International Criminal Tribunal within the framework of the trial against General Tihomir Blaskic, here present to your left, who was a colonel at the time. You were a participant, a rather important participant in the events, and we have called you to tell us about four or five matters of particular interest to us; that is, within the framework of your functions and role, which you are going to define, what was the organisation and structure of command of the 7th so-called Muslim Brigade of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, how it was deployed on the ground, what were its operations, did you know of a certain number of events, such as the kidnapping of Commander Totic, and events that took place in several Croatian villages, one of which was Dusina. Perhaps you could also speak about the fate of the prisoners and detainees which your brigade probably took in, and tell us also whether you knew, directly or indirectly, the accused. You will testify for about half an hour, a little longer, if you need, it's up to you, after which you will answer questions by the parties, the Prosecutor and the Defence, if they wish to ask you any questions, and, of course, questions by the Judges, which will come last. So, Mr. Patkovic, you may proceed about the topics you were informed of in the summons addressed to you by the Court. I wish to remind you, in view of the testimony of the previous witness, that I wish the testimony to be at the highest possible level, that your status as a witness here, you are a witness of the Chamber, not of the Prosecution or the Defence. You may, of course, refuse to make any statement that could incriminate you. However, you are obliged to answer questions put to you, but those answers cannot be used by the Office of the Prosecutor as evidence against you. The only thing may be that you may be prosecuted for perjury. So please tell us about the topics that the Chamber has asked you to comment on. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really am sorry that I wasn't able to prepare better because I received these questions in Sarajevo just before leaving for the airport, and since I've been away from Sarajevo for a long time, I have forgotten some things. The organisational structure of the 7th Brigade corresponds to a mountain brigade in terms of organisation. It had a brigade command, a staff unit, and battalions. It had three battalions which were operational, tactical units. In fact, the whole brigade was of an operative tactical nature. There was a system of subordination and command and control in accordance with the rules and regulations of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that means orders from the superior command going down to subordinate commands and commanders. During the time the brigade acted while I was commander, it operated within the zones of responsibility of the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 7th Corps because it was already of the manoeuvring type and it operated where the need arose. The area of deployment of the brigade was within the framework of the 3rd Corps in Zenica where the brigade was headquartered with the command and staff unit, a battalion in Kakanj and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Are you reading a written statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. I just have some notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is absolutely your right. And having interrupted you, would you tell us, when did you start participating in the creation of the brigade and when were you its commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I joined the 7th Muslim Brigade when it was formed. I was battalion commander. I also acted as chief of staff, and in April '94, I took over as brigade commander. I no longer recall the exact dates. So I joined when the brigade was being formed at the invitation of certain senior officers. Until then, I was commander of the Zenica detachment, which was a unit of the municipal staff of Territorial Defence of Zenica municipality. As regards combat operations, they took place in all areas of responsibility of these corps, and we acted in accordance with orders received from those commands. As for the positions I held, I was chief of staff for a very short period of time, for six months, from '93, sometime in June, July, 1993, when I was wounded, and until my appointment as commander, I was mostly on sick leave and less was I present in the unit itself. As for my perception of the conflict as a whole and the situation in the first six months of 1994, I think that the conflicts in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I was just a soldier in those days executing orders of superior command. But my perception was that it was the result of policies to split Bosnia, to destroy the state and divide it up into two, particularly '93 and '94. As for the accused, I do not know him professionally or privately nor did I ever have occasion to meet him in private life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. So that is your statement, is it not, if I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that would be my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We'll come back to it through questions which will be put to you, if necessary, by the Judges. Let me consult with my colleagues for a few minutes. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Before giving the floor to the Prosecutor and the Defence, the Chamber would like to know whether you were familiar with the events in Dusina, the kidnapping of Commander Totic, the fate of detainees and prisoners, if your brigade made any and held them in the music school. Have you heard about that? And in more general terms, the reasons that led to the formation of the 7th Muslim Brigade. After that, I will give the Prosecution and the Defence the floor. Dusina, Totic, the music school; are these points which you had to deal with in one way or another or that you heard about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, regarding Dusina, in view of the fact that a part of my battalion participated, a company, by orders from the brigade command, it was attached in the chain of command to the municipal staff, I am familiar with those events; and if I may be allowed, I shall come back to my perception of this event. As for the kidnapping of Mr. Totic, I know nothing about it. As for the formation of the 7th Muslim Brigade, I joined the brigade as a professional soldier who graduated from the military academy of the former army, and that is why I was invited to come, and I was there exclusively to help in military professional terms in the organisation of units, structuring, training, and everything else that is required for an army, and the actual reasons for the formation are not so familiar to me that I could be qualified to speak about them. So let me go back again to Dusina. Pursuant to orders of the brigade command, a unit from my battalion, which was at the time quartered in Zenica, in the barracks there, was working on a system of training, and it had just come back from an assignment in December. On the 28th of December, we had a very difficult operation at the Visoko war theatre near Sarajevo where we had many problems, a large number of people put out of action, and I carried out the reorganisation and transformation of the battalion as the brigade was in the process of being formed at the time. One company was attached to the municipal staff in the area of Lasva, which covers a broad area, including villages where one of their detachment had its command, the villages of Merdani, Dusina, Rajici, Visnjica Gornja, and Visnjica Donja. I was informed by the company commander -- by the company commander the day before the conflict broke out. Reporting to me, he briefed me on the situation in the region. They were in a region that was peaceful, but there were certain problems in the area of Merdani, as far as I was informed by the brigade command. And until then, there had been no special problems. The only problems that the company commander told me about had to do with communication with some of the soldiers when he toured units together with the commander of municipal staff units because a barricade had been put up by HVO members and so passage was not possible. But he said that all this was still not too serious. So I devoted my attention to other companies. We formed company commands, carried out training and so on. And the next day, at about 9.00, if my memory doesn't fail me, I was informed by communications that the company commander had been wounded. At that moment, I didn't understand how he had been wounded because there had been no active combat operations, and his superior command at the time was the municipal staff. Because he had been attached to that staff, I didn't quite understand what was happening. Upon receiving this information, I went to the Lasva region, which is close by, about 2 kilometres from the village of Dusina, and where I received the first information. By then, it was already noon, and I was informed that there had been an armed conflict in which my company commander had been killed together with another soldier and that there had been casualties on the other side too. I think that the HVO commander was killed as well as several soldiers. How that conflict had broken out and what was happening at the time and what I should do, I issued an order that a company that was at the time in the Zenica barracks, which means that it wasn't far away, it could reach the area of deployment within 15 or 20 minutes, that it should come and be assigned to this area where the company was. The conflict broke out when the commander went on tour, together with a group of soldiers and the commander of the municipal staff unit, towards the village of Merdani. So this conflict wasn't in the village of Dusina itself but between the village of Dusina, which was partly populated by Muslims and partly by Croats. Above the repeater, an armed conflict broke out. We assumed that this was some sort of an ambush. Due to thwarted agreements, failed agreements, an armed conflict occurred. When I reached the area, it was already over. My unit, which was up there in the village, had suffered two dead and two captured members by the HVO, and my soldiers had captured seven HVO soldiers. At that moment, there was a small house right next to the bridge over the Lasva River. I asked whether anyone was in contact with the HVO unit and its commander in Lasva. Then the people from the municipal staff told me that probably there was no communication for the time being, that they would try to establish contact. They brought the seven captured HVO members to this house. I asked what chances we had to establish contact to avoid further conflicts and to overcome problems, because if problems did occur, we were much stronger and things would become difficult. After that, there was, shall we call it, an exchange. The HVO members, who were on the ground there, and other units came as well, I'm just talking about my own units, but other units arrived, the military police of the municipal staff, an ambulance, high-level officers, and at that moment, the situation calmed down, and some HVO members surrendered. HVO units surrendered. The population stayed on in the villages. It was a mixed population. There were Croats and Bosniaks. Some had fled from Jajce when the army of Republika Srpska had expelled the population from Jajce, and I just went to the elementary school where all these people were. I came back and went to my unit. Seven HVO members who were captured were escorted to the KP Dom in Zenica, a prison which was within the jurisdiction of the corps command. I'm sorry that I didn't have time to look up the lists, but they exist, and I'm 100 per cent sure that all of them are alive. A few days ago in Zenica, I came across one of them who was captured at the time. He's currently working as a taxi driver in Busovaca. He had come as a taxi driver to Zenica, and I saw him there. So this armed conflict occurred in which there were casualties on both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Colonel Patkovic. I should now like the debate to start. Mr. Prosecutor, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I have no questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Nobilo, for the Defence, please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Patkovic. This is my colleague, Russell Hayman, and I'm Anto Nobilo, and we are Defence counsel for General Blaskic. I would like to put a few questions to you. I'm interested in the following: When did the orders to attach that company of your battalion to the Territorial Defence arrive, on what date? Can you tell me?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall the date. It came from the brigade command. I'm sure that this was before any kind of conflict and any incidents, and the date, I really cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: May I help you? Was this on the 15th of January, maybe, 1993? Because the conflict that you spoke about was the 26th of January, 1993, so could this have been eight or nine days before the conflict? Could your unit have been deployed in the area of Dusina and Lasva?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think it was that long. I don't think it was that long. I think it was only a day or two, less.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Are you sure that you were deployed there before the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: What deployment are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I'm referring to your own unit while the situation was still peaceful?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: My unit was deployed within the units of the territorial -- of the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence, that is to say, before there were any kind of conflicts, before the conflict broke out, that is to say, it was part of that unit, but it was not only deployed in the part of Dusina where there were conflicts. It wasn't deployed there at all. It was deployed in the Lasva area. Could I just clarify this a bit? I asked the commander of the municipal staff once why he wanted to reinforce his detachment there, and he said because of the Lasva loop. Parts of his unit were there, so I didn't discuss this any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you agree with the claim that the HVO never entered the village of Merdani?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you agree with the claim that the HVO never entered the village of Merdani, never took the village of Merdani?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: You're asking me about a region I do not know. I mean, I was not directly involved in such actions, and now, for me to remember something like that, no, no, I cannot say anything on that score.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us look into this very specifically. In January 1993, was the BH army or was the Territorial Defence in the village of Merdani; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please answer facing the Judges. When listening to the question, you look at counsel, but when answering, look at the Judges, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who was in the village of Merdani, the HVO or no one?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know which period you're referring to. It is mostly Bosniaks who lived in the village of Merdani.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I'm asking you about January 1993.

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: January 1993, who was in the village of Merdani? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: All right. Let's go on. When the conflicts broke out and when you received information that one of your men was wounded, can you explain to the Court why they sent information to you about the combat situation and not to those who they were attached to, the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence, and why you went to the Dusina and Lasva area and not the commander of the municipal staff from Zenica?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that this information was also received by the commander of the municipal staff, and I received this information from my own company because, after all, this is my unit which had been attached, and the officer in charge of that unit is, in a way, responsible, and it is important for me also what the situation was like in my unit. Why did I go? I went for a simple reason, to see what the situation was like in the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that when you came there, that the conflict was already over and that there were two BH army members who were imprisoned and five HVO members, and you said you were much stronger. Can you define what that meant in those villages? Who was much stronger? What was the balance of forces between the Croats and the Bosniaks when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: At that point in time -- how do I explain this? Gornja Visnjica, Donja Visnjica, Gornja Dusina, Lasva, there were mostly Bosniaks living there, that is to say, that I was referring to that segment when I said "much stronger." We wanted to avoid a conflict at all costs, that's why I said this, because it was pointless, pointless to have conflicts when we had too many conflicts with the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you came there, were you informed that certain civilians were killed?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: No, and my members did not say anything about civilians, and I do not have such information, that a single civilian was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could we please see this document -- rather, I'm going to read D434. I'm going to read a report to you, and you're going to tell me whether you know anything about this. This document is dated the 27th of January, and it comes from the Jure Francetic Brigade command.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters please have copies?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This is one of the first reports, that is to say: "On the 27th of January, 1993, displaced persons from the village of Dusine, Lasva, Local Commune, arrived in Zenica and informed us of the massacre of Croats in the above-mentioned area. "Early on the morning of 26 January 1993, MOS /Muslim liberation forces/ from Zenica surrounded seven Croatian houses in the village of Dusine. They demanded of the Dusine HVO that they surrender their weapons. After it was agreed that the demand would be honoured, MOS members opened fire on the Croatian houses. The shooting claimed the lives of the following individuals: 1. Pero Rajic ... 2. Drazenko Kegelj ... 3. Frano Rajic ... "Zvonko Rajic, son of Ivo, was killed during the negotiations. "The following two individuals were wounded: 1. Marko Rajic ... 2. Blasko Bosnjak ... "The wounded were transported to the Zenica hospital. "After the shooting ceased, MOS members entered the village, closed the civilians in the house owned by Stipe Kegelj, son of Mato, and kept them there until the night. "They arrested the HVO soldiers and seized their weapons. "After that, they started searching houses, threatening to shoot those who refuse to surrender their weapons, because they had been informed by local Muslims that there were more weapons. As they were unable to find more weapons, they carried out executions. "The following persons were shot: 1. Niko Kegelj ... 2. Vinko Kegelj ... 3. Jozo Kegelj ... 4. Mladenko Kegelj ... 5. August Rados ... "After the execution, the soldiers' bodies were taken to a cellar in a family house owned by Ivica and Jure Kegelj. "Because Marinko Kegelj ... managed to escape," this is a bit illegible, but it reads more or less as follows, "his father, Stipo Kegelj, son of Mato, was executed instead. "The following persons are still missing," and this was written on the 27th of January, 1993. "1. Perica Rados ... 2. Dragan Rados... 3. Nedjeljko Rajic ... 4. Marinko Kegelj ... "After having executed the HVO soldiers, MOS members wanted to shoot Zdravka Rados, Dragan Rados's wife. It is assumed that they abandoned their idea to carry out the execution at the request of a local Muslim. "Ivica Kegelj, son of Jure, and Milenko Rajic, son of Marko, were beaten and subjected to mistreatment and then taken towards Zenica by the BH /Bosnia and Herzegovina/ Army Military Police. Signed by the commander of the Jure Francetic Brigade, Zivko Totic. Colonel, did you hear from your soldiers about any of this?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No, not about these casualties, no. I should only say the following: Rajic --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Rajic Zvonko was the commander?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: Rajic Zvonko was the commander, and now when you read this report, perhaps I should state something. In my report, it says that there was an execution, namely, had my unit done this, I would have naturally carried out all necessary investigations. If this was within the zone of responsibility of the municipal staff, then they are in charge, and I know that the area was consolidated, naturally, by the Civil Defence, and I don't know anything about this. I'm 100 per cent sure I don't. But there is something here that I find unclear. It says on the 26th of January, 1993, in the early morning hours, the Muslim forces, MOS, from Zenica, surrounded seven Croat houses in the village of Dusina. They surrounded seven Croat houses in the village of Dusina and killed Zvonko Rajic from the village of Rajici. I think this is unclear now. According to this document and according to the report that was made by the commander of the Jure Francetic Brigade, they're saying that some village was surrounded. And then I can put a question to you: How come Zvonko Rajic was in the village of Dusina, in that house there, when he commanded an HVO unit? I mean, this doesn't -- the MOS units, I don't know which MOS units. I am commander of the 2nd Battalion of the 7th Muslim Brigade of the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Are those the only two things that surprise you in this report? Nothing else worries you?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: I am surprised. Why are you bringing this report here if this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Will you please face the Judges? This is not a polemics between you and Mr. Nobilo. It is the Judges who have summoned you to establish the truth. So please face the Judges. Afterwards, you can look at Mr. Nobilo when he puts questions to you. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: So in this report here, it is MOS units that are mentioned and also the village is surrounded and, indeed, before I was not in a position to see this report nor did I see this report nor do I consider it to be an accurate one. The Jure Francetic Brigade in Zenica was in our neighbourhood, and we could have said on time that something had happened and we could have taken care of it, but I state with full responsibility that the members of the 7th Muslim Brigade, the soldiers that were on the ground, only carried out military orders, and they absolutely did not cause any conflicts. They did not do anything to provoke others and they only could have been attacked and then they only could have defended themselves. This is shown by the fact that the first person who was killed there was the commander of the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I would like you to answer my questions, please, because our time is limited. So you told me what surprises you in this document. Of course, you hadn't seen it before and you knew nothing about this, but please tell the Court, when you came there, how many dead bodies did you see? Who was dead? You didn't say anything about that.

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: I could not see any dead bodies because the dead bodies were up on the hill and I did not climb the hill in order to consolidate the terrain and to see what was going on. It is obvious whose zone of responsibility this was, so it is only the persons who are responsible that should have inspected the corpses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: All right. Now, I would like a videotape to be played. I would like to have a videotape played, Defence Exhibit D438.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Before that, was Zvonko Rajic dead or alive when you arrived in that area?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: I know that Zvonko Rajic was dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: All right. Now let us see this video footage, that is D438. Have a look at it. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: A woman, a witness introduced this into evidence. These are the corpses from the village of Dusina that are in the morgue in Zenica. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: (Voiceover) "We are viewing the bodies of our massacred --"

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you agree that this throat has been cut here on this body? Do you agree with what I am stating?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: That is the way it looks on this video footage. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The hole here in the middle, do you agree with me that this could have been made by plucking the heart out, namely, Zvonko Rajic's heart was plucked out, according to his wife's testimony? Actually, the hole here, do you agree with me that that could be the case; that is to say, by having his heart plucked out? Do you agree that he was killed by a burst of gunfire from an automatic rifle? You could know this. You are a professional soldier.

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: That it was a burst of gunfire?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But if you look at the entry wounds, was it an automatic rifle; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: It's hard to tell now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. We are no longer going to view this tape because we haven't got much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did any of your subordinates describe to you how Rajic got killed? Your subordinates, did they explain how this HVO commander got killed?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: It's very difficult to recall fully that situation. I know that it was a very hard situation, and I know what the situation was like in my unit because the commander of my unit had been killed. We did not discuss this very much. We know that there was an armed conflict which we had not caused, which our men had not caused, and which had a tragic outcome for both sides. Soldiers were killed on both sides. This was purely an armed conflict. And how all of this had happened, it would be very, very difficult to analyse it now and to remember, ultimately, various details, or to have someone to describe this faithfully. As for my soldiers, we did not discuss this very much. We did not discuss this subject very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: All right. Of course, a lot of time has gone by, so I shall try to jog your memory. Is it true that when you came, you went to a place called Brdo where HVO soldiers were, that you put women and children in front of you as a human shield and then, in that way, you tried to take that position where HVO soldiers were; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: That is a lie. That is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is it correct that after that, you called Zvonko Rajic and guaranteed his safety and that you asked him to come for negotiations, and when he came for negotiations and when he put down his arms so that you could talk, that you personally jumped at him and grabbed him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: No, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is it true that you brought Zvonko Rajic to the building of the local community and used your pistol and shot at his upper right leg?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: That is not true. Zvonko Rajic was already dead when I arrived on the spot. I said that earlier on. Please. I am a professional soldier who has been in many battlefields of Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes. You're a witness here, so please answer my questions. You were a soldier in the war. Is it true that you shot at the other foot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, you are a witness, I must remind you, and I will remind you of the rules, that you can refuse to answer a question if you think it could incriminate you. But the Chamber needs to know a certain number of things and provides all the guarantees to you. That being so, the Judges wish to hear your version of events. Mr. Nobilo, rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. Patkovic, is it true that you killed Zvonko Rajic and emptied your pistol into him?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is it true that an HVO soldier, Dragan Rados, you pointed your pistol at him, the pistol clicked, but there were no bullets in there, and then you said to him, "You're free. Allah," or God, "has saved you." Is that true?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I would like to ask my learned friend Mr. Hayman to read a statement that Their Honours have heard here in the courtroom and then I will ask you my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Reporter's transcript, page 14940, line 20: Q How did he tell you that? A When Patkovic came, I was sitting, and he said, "See, Zvonko took care of his family, and he left you to be killed by us." And a friend of mine, a lady, said, "That is not true. Zvonko did not take care of his family at all. His wife and child are here." He looked at me, he sat down, he sat on a table there, perhaps this was about half a metre away from me, and he said, "Mrs. Rajic, I can describe your husband now, what he's wearing." I was looking at him, and I really felt lost. I wondered why he was telling me all of this. He described my husband, that he had a helmet on his head, that he had a flak jacket on, that he had a Skorpio, that he had a camouflage jacket, like all other soldiers, and he said that he fired an entire round into his head and that afterwards they committed a massacre. Q You mean over your husband's body? A Yes, that is what I meant ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The witness, in this court under oath, like you are now, said this. Did you describe to the witness her husband in this way? Did you say this?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I never said anything like that nor did I do that. How could I say something I hadn't done?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The same witness, in continuation of her testimony, described how you came to talk to them and to amuse them; and then after a time, you took a man out, a shot would be heard, and he would be dead. After that, you would come back again, and again you would talk to them, try to change the subject, and in this way, you took out one man after another. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What do you think, generally speaking, a woman who loses her husband, what could be her motive to falsely accuse anyone? What would be her motive?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that and I wouldn't speculate about anybody's motives. I know what I did or, rather, what I didn't do, and what she said is a lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How would you comment on the fact that that witness, sitting where you are sitting now, recognised the killer of her husband, knew on the basis of a photograph published in the Bosnian newspaper? Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: How can I comment on somebody -- would you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: She recognised you on a photograph published in the newspaper just then when she was testifying here, and this was your first interview after the war, and seeing that photograph, she recognised you as the killer of her husband. So she even recognised your face, not only your name. How would you interpret that?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know nor can I interpret it in any way one way or another. I am saying that that is a lie, I didn't do that, nor were there any objective circumstances enabling me to do that. The conflicts occurred before I arrived, Mr. Rajic was already dead, and that woman, or that witness, I never saw her nor did I talk to her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Will you please proceed to another type of question? We have about fifteen or twenty minutes. I must remind you that this is not a trial of Mr. Patkovic. On the other hand, it is quite normal for you to ask questions to illustrate the credibility or non-credibility of the witness in connection with the charges against Colonel Blaskic. But I must remind you that this is not a trial of Colonel Patkovic. It was in response to the wishes of the Judges that the witnesses come, and he has come to talk about the 7th Muslim Brigade, and, of course, you have every right to know what that brigade did in the context of your defence strategy. So please proceed, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Actually, I'm almost done. I have one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was an investigation conducted about this crime in the 7th Brigade or any other war crime committed by the 7th Muslim Brigade ever?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: The 7th Muslim Brigade did not commit crimes, and while I was commander of the brigade, after every operation, it was analysed by the command, and the 7th Muslim Brigade did not commit crimes. It was the most honourable brigade of the BH army. People joined it wholeheartedly, respecting all international norms, respect of ethics, belief in God and man. So this is simply a fabrication and I don't understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Those things are not being imputed by Mr. Nobilo. I must remind you that Mr. Nobilo is not the Prosecutor. What does interest us, however, is whether you are testifying falsely or whether the witness herself, who came here a few months ago, was testifying falsely. This could be the object of an investigation because there are procedures for perjury. Nothing is being alleged here. Mr. Nobilo is defending an accused and he needs to investigate certain facts, and I told Mr. Nobilo that he should stop regarding that particular point. Mr. Nobilo, have you any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, because you have heard sufficient about what the Defence considers to be crimes by the 7th Muslim Brigade. Wherever they appeared, there were massive crimes, and I wouldn't like to tire this Chamber with further testimony of this kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You are not tiring us, you are not abusing our time. This is all part of the Blaskic trial, and the Judges are here to hear the Defence case as well as the Prosecution case as well as what the accused may have to tell us. Let me turn to my colleagues now. Judge Shahabuddeen? No questions. Judge Rodrigues, have you any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Rodrigues has the floor

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Colonel Patkovic, in the 7th Brigade, was there any kind of special discipline or anything like that? You said that the 7th Brigade was different in relation to all the other brigades. What did that difference consist of?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: It was different in relation to other brigades because it was more responsible in executing its tasks. All tasks assigned to us were carried out on time. And within the system of control and command, when you have a brigade of that kind, we were a pillar of support for everyone. We were a brigade that showed professionalism from the very beginning in executing its tasks, on the ground, in the barracks, when going on leave, and in every other respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Because of its special tasks, there was a special training and discipline or not?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: No, nothing special, no special training, that did not exist, but as for special discipline, according to the rules in the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were disciplinary regulations for soldiers of units. They could not drink alcohol, and in that respect, measures were very strict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Regarding the training of the 7th Brigade, were there training camps?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: The training centres existed within the framework of units within the corps. All the training centres in the corps were training centres for the brigade, and within the framework of battalions and other units, we just had practice, drill. Since a manoeuvring brigade is on the ground, one company would stay in reserve for additional training of new recruits because we were reinforcing units because of losses in battle, and all the training centres were those that existed within the 3rd Corps of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: It was the 7th Muslim Brigade by name. Why this name? Why was it called the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't name it, so I really couldn't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: When you arrived, the name already existed?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: But was there a 6th or an 8th Muslim Brigade or only this particular brigade had this qualification of "Muslim"?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: No, there were other Muslim brigades. There was the 4th within the 4th Corps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting you, Colonel. So there were other brigades that were called the 4th Muslim Brigade, for instance?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Something else now. Did international organisations visit the brigade or not?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Which organisations visited your brigade?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: While I was brigade commander, members of SFOR came, I know that for sure, I think from the Spanish Battalion, that's as far as I can recollect, and all the other organisations that came would visit the brigade, just as they did all other units, through the corps or directly to the brigade, but they did come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You said that while you were commander, that means after April 1994?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: Before that too, but I can't talk on behalf of someone else because I was not so familiar with things because I spent most of my time on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Something else. The uniforms worn by the members of this brigade, were they the same as those worn by members of other brigades or were they different?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: They were absolutely the same as the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Because somebody told us that the uniforms of the 7th Brigade differed, that they were white with other accessories that other brigades did not have.

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: Some white uniforms were covers, white covers, but they were used by other brigades as well. They were white covers worn over camouflage uniforms because of the winter, and during parades, these white uniforms would sometimes be worn. They were covers, really, for the line-up of brigades, for ceremonial events, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, but we received information that members of the brigade most of the time were dressed in white with a green bandanna around their heads, so that is not true?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: That was only for ceremonies. Some members would be dressed in that way but not all. But in military terms, it would be absurd for soldiers to go into combat in white uniform because they are highly visible then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: But you admit that this kind of clothing may have been used for certain ceremonies?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: That was used by other units as well. I don't know if you're aware of the parade of the 3rd Corps. All units were differently dressed. This was specific to each brigade. Each brigade, in addition to the insignia of the corps, which had to be indicated on the uniform, the emblem of the brigade could have been worn. That was according to the regulations of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: How could people distinguish the 7th Brigade members from another brigade?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: On the ground, it was very difficult. One could not tell the difference. There were no differences, actually, because many soldiers transferred from the 7th to the 303rd and vice versa; they were the same men. But an image developed of the 7th Brigade because of the successes it had on the ground. It was a brigade that fully executed its tasks. In the system of defence, we were invincible, and as for all other tasks, we fulfilled them completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: But when a brigade was engaged in combat operations, there were no insignia or anything else to identify it?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: No. Perhaps on the uniform, somebody would wear the brigade emblem but nothing that was particularly conspicuous and that distinguished it from others, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: So a person could recognise the presence of the 7th Brigade by the consequences of its actions only. I'm sorry. You said that people recognised the 7th Brigade because it was very effective, it accomplished its missions well, and that is how people recognised the 7th.

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I wasn't talking about recognition in that way. I said that it created an image about that brigade, but, in fact, it was no different than the other brigades. There wasn't any major difference. But in the stories circulating, I remember when I took over as commander, 400 men from my brigade were transferred to another brigade, and I had fresh reinforcements because we became a manoeuvring brigade. So they couldn't be recognised on the ground, but there was more rumour about it than there was real fact behind this recognition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, but one says, when one sees the smoke, there must be a fire, but in relation to the participation of foreign members, were there any members of the 7th Brigade who came from abroad?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: If I ask you more specifically, were there any Mujahedin, people known as Mujahedin, public opinion made this up, that there were Mujahedin in the 7th Muslim Brigade; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: Allow me to clarify. There were members of the 7th Muslim Brigade, a small number of them, who wore beards, so this would be designated in a platoon, and then when they saw somebody from another unit, they would say, "There's a Mujahedin." But, no, there were no Mujahedins in our brigade during the time I was commander of battalion and commander of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Colonel, who financed the 7th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: The corps, the 3rd Corps of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Only? Only the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: According to the system of distribution of resources, the 3rd Corps of the BH army, and for the rest, we managed somehow to get some resources from other sources. I never received a salary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: What about the Islamic Centre?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: The Islamic Centre is a humanitarian organisation, and before I took over as brigade commander and before I joined the brigade, people who used to work in the organisation of the army, and through the Muslim forces, they worked in the Islamic Centre, so there was some kind of a connection between them. But in the system of control and command and deployment of the brigade and the financing and everything, it had nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Rodrigues. I think that we have finished, Colonel. I have one question only for you. In view of what happened in Dusina, you abide by what you said under oath today, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SERIF PATKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for coming. At the end of the day, I should like to stress once again, and I say that on behalf of my colleagues, that I'm appreciative of the cooperation of your government which has contributed to the good functioning of the International Criminal Tribunal in summoning the witnesses, the group of witnesses of which you are a member. Don't move, Colonel, for the moment. Mr. Fourmy, I think we meet again on Tuesday at 2.30, don't we, at 2.00 or 2.30?

utterances.speaker: MR. FOURMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Perhaps we could ask the Defence what their plan is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fourmy. You think of everything. Mr. Hayman, Tuesday afternoon, are we going to have your witnesses, character witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, good afternoon. We have cleared Tuesday afternoon with two of the three witnesses in terms of their professional calendars. We're working with the Registrar's office to get visas for those two, and we expect them to be here. If there is some problem, perhaps there is a contact on Monday, I know Monday is -- is Monday a holiday? It may be a holiday. If the court is open on Monday, obviously, if there is any problem, we will inform your staff properly, but we expect two --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, it is open Monday, but we cannot have hearings, at least as far as I'm concerned, so the hearing is for Tuesday, 2.30, and, of course, we hope to have your witnesses. If, by any chance, I address Mr. Fourmy, if we don't have those witnesses, could we perhaps examine the exhibits, whose destiny is still uncertain? Mr. Prosecutor, would that be possible, to take advantage of the afternoon for that, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We will now adjourn. Mr. Fourmy? Thank you, Mr. Fourmy. We are sitting on Tuesday at 2.00 p.m., from 2.00 to 6.00. I say that for the benefit of my colleagues, but let me see if they agree first. Judge Shahabuddeen, do you agree? Judge Rodrigues? Yes. Very well. Thank you. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
